title: Honen
hookLine: the Japanese monk who taught the nembutsu, calling Amida's name, for everyone

lines: THE FISHERMAN, THE FARMER, THE MOTHER.
cards: A fisherman can't stop fishing to sit in meditation. A farmer can't memorize the sutras between harvests. A mother with small children has no hours to spend in a temple hall.
A monk on a Japanese mountain, a careful and learned scholar, kept asking what the Buddha's teaching could offer people like them.

And, his life stories say, he asked it about himself too, because he felt he could not keep the hard practices perfectly either. The answer he found was so short that anyone could carry it: a name, said with trust.

teach.b: First, the Buddha he turned to. The Pure Land sutras tell of a Buddha named Amitabha, Amida in Japanese, who long ago vowed to bring into his Pure Land any being who calls on him with trust.

One of those sutras explains the name: his light is immeasurable, shining without obstruction everywhere. Second, the turning point. Honen had studied for years on Mount Hiei, a great center of learning.

Tradition says that reading a commentary by the Chinese teacher Shandao, he came on a line about holding Amida's name in mind single-heartedly, walking, standing, sitting or lying down, and he understood that this was the practice Amida's vow itself had chosen.
Not one practice among many to be added on. The one. Third, the words.
The nembutsu, in Japanese, is Namu Amida Butsu: I take refuge in Amida Buddha.
Honen taught that saying it with trust is enough, and that it is open to everyone, learned or not, monk or lay, man or woman, good or struggling.
Near the end of his life he wrote a short statement for his students, and it says, in essence: no need for deep learning; just say the name. Fourth, what it cost.
His teaching drew strong opposition from older schools, and for a time he was sent into exile. The community that grew from him, the Pure Land school, Jodo Shu, still keeps the name at its heart.

how: Followers of Jodo Shu, the Pure Land school that traces itself to Honen, recite Namu Amida Butsu at home and in temple services, sometimes counting recitations on prayer beads.

games.q: you're Honen. you've studied for years and still can't keep every hard practice perfectly. then you read Shandao's line about holding Amida's name in mind. what do you conclude?
o: add the name to all the other practices
the name, said with trust, is the practice
games.why: Honen concluded that calling Amida's name was the practice Amida's vow itself had chosen, open to everyone.

practice: If you pray, say one short prayer you already know, slowly, letting each word land; if you walk the Pure Land path, that may be Namu Amida Butsu.

If you don't pray, choose a plain phrase you trust, the name of someone who loves you, or simply the words thank you, and let it ride the out-breath, again and again, with no need to understand it all.

wordCard.voice: Honen. The Japanese monk who taught that calling Amida's name with trust, the nembutsu, is open to everyone. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese Namu Amida Butsu: I take refuge in Amida Buddha. the nembutsu Honen taught.

carryVoice: Your line: just the name. Open to everyone, learned or not. That's day nine hundred ninety-two.
